html:
The Hausa Kingdoms were a group of walled city-states between the Niger River and Lake Chad, in what is now northern Nigeria. The map shows them from 1492 to 1800.

According to the legend of Bayajidda, a hero from Baghdad killed a snake in a well at Daura and married its queen; their descendants founded the seven "true" Hausa states, among them Daura, Kano, Katsina, Zazzau (Zaria), Gobir, Rano and Biram.

Each state was built around a walled city with a market. Their wealth came from farming, cotton cloth dyed with indigo, leather and long-distance trade:

  • south to the forest for kola nuts and gold, through markets such as Kurmi Market in Kano;
  • north across the desert in the trans-Saharan trade.

Islam arrived with traders and scholars in the 1300s and 1400s and spread among rulers and merchants. The states fought each other often and at times paid tribute to Kanem-Bornu or Songhai, but none united them all.

That came from outside. In 1804 the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio declared a jihad against the Hausa kings, whom he called lax Muslims. By 1808 he had taken Gobir, and the Hausa cities became emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate. Hausa is today the most widely spoken language of West Africa.
sum: The Hausa Kingdoms were a group of walled city-states between the Niger River and Lake Chad, in what is now northern Nigeria. The map shows them from 1492 to 1800.
